About the only sense of cause in mathematics is logical implication. As long as you avoid circular reasoning, there won’t be a violation of causality. Dedekind used this to define a real number as what we now call a Dedekind cut of rational numbers. For Dedekind, a real number is something that separates rational numbers m / n into two nonempty sets, the elements of one subset (the left subset) being less than or equal to all the elements of the other subset (the right subset). There are two distinctions between Eudoxus’ concept and Dedekind’s concept. First, Eudoxus only considered positive magnitudes and positive ratios while Dedekind allowed for ratios to be zero or negative. The second is that Eudoxus required magnitudes to define ratios, but Dedekind’s concept was more abstract so didn’t require preexisting magnitudes for real numbers.
